newsitem.title: USA: Clinton plan adds $80 billion in taxes.
newsitem.headline: Clinton plan adds $80 billion in taxes.

text.p: President Clinton's tax plan will include $80 billion in tax increases over five years achieved by closing corporate loopholes and extending expiring taxes, a congressional aide said Friday.

Administration officials briefed Democrats on the tax proposals which were said to be much the same as those the White House proposed in last year's budget. The money would offset an estimated $100 billion in tax cuts through 2002.
One of the most controversial would require investment owners to use "average cost basis" to compute capital gains taxes, a more restrictive method of counting stock sold.
The congressional aide said administration officials briefed Democratic staff on closures of corporate tax breaks which would raise about $39 billion over five years.

However, unlike Clinton's fiscal 1997 budget, this year's proposal would not require investors to use "average cost basis" until the law takes effect, the aide said. Clinton's 1997 plan provided for $59 billion in corporate loophole closures.

Another profitable tax break for investors, called "selling short against the box" would be eliminated in Clinton's plan. Rather than selling stock that is owned, investors are able to sell identical stock they have borrowed with their own stock used as collateral.
Clinton is also to seek renewal of airport trust fund taxes which expired Dec. 31 including the 10 percent excise tax on tickets.
The tax also adds 6.25 percent to air cargo bills, adds $6 per ticket for international departures and addes 15 cents per gallon to aviation gas and 17.5 cents per gallon on jet fuel.
Sen. John McCain, R-Ariz, introduced legislation Thursday to extend the tax through December 1997.
In addition, Treasury officials said Clinton's plan would repeal the subsidy multinational companies receive for exports to foreign units.
As in last year's White House budget, the plan will also restrict interest deductions companies get from investments in tax-exempt bonds.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, found it an "unwelcome" sign that details of the Administration's tax proposal were given to the public and not to Republicans in Congress, a senior House Republican aide said.
"Republicans were not informed of any of the information," the aide said.
